Antiquity
ăn-tĭk´wĭ-ty
n. (ancientness; former ages; the authority claimed for age; rendering Hebrew qadmah)
Latin antiquitas, from antiquus, ancient. In the controversies of the Reformation the word names an argument: that a doctrine is proved by having been believed a long time.

Biblical Definition

Isaiah uses the word of Tyre: “Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn” (Isa 23:7) — and the age of the city did not save it. Scripture commends the old paths where they are God's: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). It equally condemns the antiquity of an error: the fathers who tempted God in the wilderness are a warning, not a precedent (Psa 95:8–9), and “your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever?” (Zec 1:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines antiquity as ancient times; former ages; great age; the people of ancient times; and remains of ancient times.

expand to see more

ANTIQUITY, n. Ancient times; former ages; times long since past.

2. The ancients; the people of ancient times.

3. Ancientness; great age; the quality of being ancient.

4. Remains of ancient times.

Key Scripture

Isa 23:7 — "Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn."

Jer 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Zec 1:5 — "Your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever?"

Psa 95:8 — "Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness:"

Mar 7:8 — "For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do."

Modern Corruption

Age is offered as proof of truth, and Jeremiah's old paths are commended for being God's, not for being old.

expand to see more

The appeal to antiquity was Rome's strongest instinctive argument and it remains the most persuasive one: this is what has always been believed, and you are new. The Reformers answered it in two ways. First by disputing the history — showing that the practices in question were not primitive but medieval, and that the fathers they were charged with abandoning could be quoted against Trent. Second, and more fundamentally, by denying that age settles the question at all. Tradition is a witness and not a judge; the Bereans searched the scriptures daily to see whether the things Paul preached were so, and Paul was an apostle.

Jeremiah 6:16 is the verse most often quoted for the other side, and it does commend the old paths — but the sentence names the test in its middle clause: ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein. The antiquity and the goodness are two separate questions, and Jeremiah expects the enquirer to ask both. Mark 7:8 shows what happens when only the first is asked: laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, and the tradition there was old, respected, and universally kept.

The Protestant version of the error is nostalgia — a settled conviction that some earlier decade of one's own denomination was the golden age, and that recovery means returning to it. Zechariah 1:5 is the cure, and it is bracing: your fathers, where are they? and the prophets, do they live for ever? The fathers are dead and the word is not; the next verse says the word took hold of them. What survives an age is what was true in it, and the only way to find that out is to go back past every antiquity to the text.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qadmah (H6927), antiquity, former state; olam (H5769), long duration, ancient time; Greek paradosis (G3862), tradition, that which is handed down.

expand to see more

Hebrew qadmah (H6927) — antiquity, former state; Isaiah 23:7, Ezekiel 16:55.

Hebrew netivot olam (H5410, H5769) — the old paths, ancient ways; Jeremiah 6:16, 18:15.

Greek paradosis (G3862) — tradition; Mark 7:8–9, Colossians 2:8, 2 Thessalonians 2:15.

Usage

"“Whose antiquity is of ancient days” — and her feet carried her away."

"“Ask for the old paths, where is the good way” — two questions, not one."

"“Your fathers, where are they?” — the cure for nostalgia."
